finalAnswer: Simulate each cane with a monotone lower endpoint; stop when it is consumed. At most 30 canes require scanning past the first cow.
shortExplanation: Track the height of the first uneaten piece. Most canes finish at the first cow, and every unfinished one doubles that cow’s height, which bounds the number of expensive scans.
detailedSteps: For one cane of height $c$, let $b=0$ be its uneaten lower endpoint. A cow whose height before her turn is $h$ eats $e=\max(0,\min(h,c)-b)$. Then increase $b$ by $e$. The remaining interval stays suspended at its original height.

Update that cow to height $h+e$, retaining her old height when computing $e$. The source delays growth until the cane ends, but each cow visits only once; immediate updates therefore give exactly the same result. As soon as $b=c$, the rest of the cows eat nothing and the loop stops.

If the first cow cannot finish a cane, $c>h_1$ and she eats $h_1$, doubling her height. All cane heights are at most $10^9$. Starting from a positive integer height, this can occur at most 30 times; after that, the first cow finishes every remaining cane.

The work is $O(M+N\log C_{\max})$, rather than $O(NM)$. The implementation streams cane heights and stores only the cow heights, using $O(N)$ extra space. A final height is bounded by its initial height plus the sum of all cane heights, so use 64-bit integers.
keyIdeas: Keep the unconsumed interval’s lower endpoint.
Charge every full scan to a doubling of the first cow.
commonMistakes: Do not lower the remaining cane to the ground.
Use the cow’s pre-turn height before updating her growth.
Avoid scanning all cows after the cane is gone.
alternativeMethods: A deferred-growth simulation gives the same small-case results and is useful as an independent testing oracle. Its unoptimized worst-case running time is too large.
difficultyNotes: The implementation is short, but a complete solution needs the amortized bound. The source’s samples, exhaustive small probes and official test files are audited separately; no online judge submission is claimed.

finalAnswer: For each infected run of length $L$, add $\lceil L/(2T+1)\rceil$, where $T$ is the largest time allowed by every run. Return 0 for no infected cows and 1 when all cows are infected.
shortExplanation: Zeros limit how long the infection could have spread. Use the greatest common feasible number of nights, then cover each run with as few infection intervals as possible.
detailedSteps: After $T$ nights, one initial infection reaches every position at distance at most $T$, clipped only at the physical ends of the line. A final zero can never lie in such an interval.

For a run of $L$ ones surrounded by zeros, a seed needs room on both sides, so $T\le\lfloor(L-1)/2\rfloor$. A run touching exactly one end of the line permits $T\le L-1$. The all-zero and all-one strings are separate immediate cases.

Take the minimum of these bounds across all runs. Time is shared by the whole line, not chosen independently for each run. Set $w=2T+1$. Each seed covers at most $w$ cows, so a run needs at least $q=\lceil L/w\rceil$ seeds.

This bound is attainable. In an interior run, put the first and last seed centers $T$ positions from the two zero boundaries. The admissible center span has width $L-w\le(q-1)w$, so $q$ centers with gaps at most $w$ cover the run without crossing a zero. For a run at one physical end, start $T$ positions from its zero-side boundary and continue toward the physical end with gaps at most $w$; the last interval may be clipped there. The time bound guarantees that this placement fits.

The minimum seeds for each run are therefore $\lceil L/w\rceil$. This expression never increases when feasible $T$ increases, so the largest feasible shared $T$ minimizes the total. Find runs and sum the counts in $O(N)$ time; this implementation stores $O(N)$ run lengths.
keyIdeas: An infection expands as a clipped interval.
A zero imposes a hard boundary.
Optimize one shared time before counting seeds.
commonMistakes: Do not treat a physical line end as an uninfected cow.
Different runs cannot use different numbers of nights.
If an internal run is very short, it can force zero nights for every run.
alternativeMethods: For small lines, enumerate every initial infection mask and evolve it night by night. This provides a structurally different correctness oracle, but is exponential.
difficultyNotes: The main work is proving both necessity and attainability of the run bounds. The all-one string has no zero boundary; it should not be subjected to an internal-run bound.

finalAnswer: Invert the target ranks and intersect the adjacent integer inequalities. Output the smallest feasible day $d\ge0$, or $-1$ if the interval is empty.
shortExplanation: A target permutation specifies a strict height order. Adjacent plants alone determine that order, and each adjacent pair gives a lower or upper bound on the integer day.
detailedSteps: Let $p[r]$ be the index with target rank $r$, where rank 0 is tallest. The request holds exactly when $H_{p[0]}(d)>H_{p[1]}(d)>\cdots>H_{p[N-1]}(d)$. Adjacent strict comparisons are necessary and, by transitivity, sufficient.
For consecutive indices $i,j$, integer heights turn strictness into $h_i+a_i d\ge h_j+a_j d+1$. Write $A=a_i-a_j$ and $B=h_j-h_i+1$; then $Ad\ge B$. The extra 1 excludes ties.

If $A>0$, impose $d\ge\lceil B/A\rceil$. If $A<0$, impose $d\le\lfloor B/A\rfloor$. If $A=0$, this pair is possible only when $B\le0$. Start with lower bound 0 and no upper bound, and intersect every pair’s requirement.

If any equal-rate pair is impossible, or the final lower bound exceeds the upper bound, return $-1$. Otherwise the lower bound satisfies all pairs and is the first feasible day. For a single plant there are no pair constraints, so the answer is 0.

Build the inverse permutation and inspect $N-1$ pairs in $O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ space. Use exact signed floor and ceiling division with 64-bit integers. Global binary search is inappropriate: faster lower-ranked plants can impose an upper bound, making the feasible days a bounded interval.
keyIdeas: Strict integer inequalities need a one-unit gap.
Intersect lower and upper day bounds.
commonMistakes: A tie never satisfies two distinct target ranks.
Negative division in C++ truncates toward zero, which is not always floor.
A feasible-day predicate need not remain true forever.
alternativeMethods: Brute-force days and all pairwise ranks on bounded small inputs for a separate oracle. Sorting by target rank also works, but an inverse permutation avoids its extra logarithmic cost.
difficultyNotes: The proof must handle positive, negative and zero slope differences separately. It is not enough to keep only the time when each desired taller plant first catches its neighbor.
